item.title: “I think I need a break...": Robert Eggers opens up about stepping away from horror
item.description: Filmmaker Robert Eggers is ready to step away from the horror genre after more than a decade of exploring witches, vampires and werewolves on screen.
item.content:encoded:
“I think I need a break...": Robert Eggers opens up about stepping away from horror Filmmaker Robert Eggers is ready to step away from the horror genre after more than a decade of exploring witches, vampires and werewolves on screen. ANI | Updated: 23-11-2026 15:18 IST | Created: 23-11-2026 15:18 IST

Robert Eggers (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Filmmaker Robert Eggers is ready to step away from the horror genre after more than a decade of exploring witches, vampires and werewolves on screen. As per Deadline, the director has expressed his desire to move beyond what he calls “Robert Eggers’ House of Horror” and explore other genres with his next project. “I’m eager not to continue purposely doing Robert Eggers’ House of Horror,” Eggers said during a recent Q&A, adding, “I don’t need to do the Mummy or The Opera. Not to say that I won’t, but I think I need a break.” Eggers' comments come amid recent discussions with Focus Features about an adaptation of William Shakespeare’s 'Romeo & Juliet'. The filmmaker described the potential project as “a break” from the horror film he had been planning to make next. Explaining what prompted him to reconsider his immediate filmmaking plans, Eggers said he had initially started writing another horror film after Werwulf. However, the material became increasingly dark, making him realise that he wanted to try something different. “I was doing something else,” noted Eggers, adding, “But what happened was, after Werwulf, I was writing another horror movie, and it got so dark again, and I was like, ‘I need a break. So, I’ll do something about two teenagers killing themselves,'” as cited by Deadline. Since making his feature directorial debut with The Witch in 2015, Eggers has established himself as a prominent filmmaker in the horror genre. His filmography includes The Lighthouse (2019), Nosferatu (2024) and his latest film, Werwulf. Werwulf, which premieres in theatres on December 25 from Focus Features, is set in 14th-century England. The film follows a man, played by Aaron Taylor-Johnson, whose family faces a threat from a ravenous beast haunting their town. The film also features Lily-Rose Depp, Willem Dafoe and Ralph Ineson, among others. (ANI)

item.title: ROI-Fintech poised to redraw the global investment map: Kamal Bhatia
item.description: When Venetian merchant Marco Polo encountered paper money in 13th-century China, he saw proof of the empire's economic sophistication.
item.content:encoded:
ROI-Fintech poised to redraw the global investment map: Kamal Bhatia When Venetian merchant Marco Polo encountered paper money in 13th-century China, he saw proof of the empire's economic sophistication. Reuters | Updated: 23-11-2026 12:30 IST | Created: 23-11-2026 12:30 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

When Venetian merchant Marco Polo encountered paper money in 13th-century China, he saw proof of the empire's economic sophistication. Today, digital financial infrastructure offers a similarly powerful signal of a country’s growth potential. Investors have traditionally approached fintech from the bottom up, seeking innovative companies and disruptive business models, but increasingly, there is a top-down consideration too: which countries are building the most sophisticated digital financial infrastructure to give their economies a competitive advantage? Fintech – the use of technology to improve the delivery of financial services – is bringing more people into the formal economy globally, changing how quickly money moves, expanding households' and businesses' financial access, and helping to channel domestic savings into productive investment. But the rate of adoption diverges significantly across geographies. Investors seeking to target markets with significant growth potential, therefore, now have another metric to consider beyond inflation, fiscal sustainability, demographics, valuations or institutional quality: fintech development. NEW-WAVE AMBITION Getting a larger portion of a country’s population into the official financial sector and channeling more domestic savings into productive investment have always been key to economic growth – but doing so in the 21st century increasingly requires digital financial innovation. Principal Financial Group’s latest Global Financial Inclusion Index bears this out. It finds that financial system support was the strongest source of improvement across the 42 markets we benchmark for financial inclusion. The public sector plays a critical role. Government investment in digital infrastructure, skills, funding, regulation and AI can determine whether private-sector innovation is able to scale. Done well, public and private investment can reinforce one another, creating a virtuous cycle. Innovation attracts capital, capital strengthens the economy, and stronger economies expand productive capacity. Saudi Arabia is a prime example of how fintech can become economic policy, rather than simply financial-sector policy. The kingdom has garnered attention recently because of the wars in the Middle East, yet, despite the turmoil in the region, it continues to move forward with a bold roadmap for economic transformation. Saudi Arabia is more than halfway through its Vision 2030 plan, a state-led diversification strategy that seeks to attract hundreds of billions of dollars in investment to reduce the economy's reliance on hydrocarbon revenue. Within that agenda, Saudi Arabia has paired fintech targets with investment in regulation, skills and digital infrastructure, aiming to host 525 fintech companies, create about 18,000 sector jobs and attract 12 billion riyals ($3.2 billion) in venture investment by 2030. Saudi Arabia is already ahead of its interim milestones. By the end of 2024, the kingdom had 261 fintech companies operating, exceeding its 2025 target of 230 a year early. Its ambition has helped to attract significant investor interest. EY’s 2025 Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Attractiveness Survey found that Saudi Arabia captured the region's largest share of announced foreign direct investment (FDI) capital in 2024. Of course, the conflict in the Gulf may hamper investment temporarily, but it is unlikely to reverse long-term positive trends on the fintech front, which should enable the kingdom to continue differentiating itself. Latin America is also seeing a marked rise in financial inclusion, and it is no coincidence that this region has also seen an explosion in digital infrastructure, from Brazil's Pix instant payment system to Argentina's Transferencias 3.0. Colombia, in particular, stands out. Despite a less mature fintech ecosystem, it has taken a bold approach by building Bre-B, an interoperable instant payments system. It is also home to some of Latin America's most promising fintech companies, giving it the potential to become one of the region's leading hubs for financial innovation. Other markets well positioned to benefit from fintech development include India, Hong Kong and the US. OLD-WORLD INERTIA By contrast, several European Union economies are struggling. Six of the bloc's 10 member states in our index saw their financial system rankings fall this year: Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark, Italy, Spain and Poland. Meanwhile, businesses in several major EU economies are among the least likely to use AI to enhance employees' financial support and benefits. This old-world inertia could have real economic consequences. The EU's Savings and Investments Union, launched last year, seeks to address the bloc’s age-old problem of turning large pools of household cash into investment that could reinvigorate growth. But legacy tech is surely part of what is holding it back. None of this suggests that fintech development should displace traditional metrics when assessing countries’ economic growth potential. Nor does an ambitious government fintech strategy guarantee successful execution. But, over time, the countries that treat fintech as economic infrastructure should be better placed to attract international capital and ultimately redraw the global investment map. (The views expressed here are those of Kamal Bhatia, CEO of Principal Asset Management.) Enjoying this column? Check out Reuters Open Interest (ROI), your essential new source for global financial commentary. Follow ROI on LinkedIn, and X. And listen to the Morning Bid daily podcast on Apple, Spotify, or the Reuters app. Subscribe to hear Reuters journalists discuss the biggest news in markets and finance seven days a week. ($1 = 3.7533 riyals) (By Kamal Bhatia; Editing by Marguerita Choy and Anna Szymanski)

item.title: Vietnam’s New Land Law Could Speed Up Priority Projects but Weaken Farmers’ Bargaining Power
item.description: Vietnam’s revised land law, effective July 2027, could speed up priority projects by allowing some land acquisition decisions before compensation plans are approved. The change could weaken farmers’ ...
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam’s New Land Law Could Speed Up Priority Projects but Weaken Farmers’ Bargaining Power Vietnam’s revised land law, effective July 2027, could speed up priority projects by allowing some land acquisition decisions before compensation plans are approved. The change could weaken farmers’ bargaining power, putting pressure on provincial authorities to value land fairly, resolve objections and pay households on time. Devdiscourse News Desk | Updated: 22-11-2026 13:53 IST | Created: 22-11-2026 13:53 IST

Representative Image.

Country:

Vietnam

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Vietnam's National Assembly approved a revised land law on November 21, giving authorities a faster route to acquire land for certain projects. The law generally takes effect on July 1, 2027, and was passed with 466 of 479 participating deputies voting in favour. For Vietnam, the potential gain is more predictable delivery of infrastructure and industrial projects. For farmers and other land users, the change raises a more immediate question: how much influence will they have over compensation once authorities can issue an acquisition decision before the payment plan is final?

Faster land clearance could give Vietnam more predictable project timelines Land disputes can delay projects when households challenge compensation offers they consider below market value. The revised law addresses one source of delay by changing the order of decisions. In eligible cases, authorities can issue a land acquisition decision before approving the compensation plan. An earlier National Assembly resolution already allowed accelerated land recovery in some circumstances, including for nationally important projects ordered to proceed faster and urgent public investment projects. The revised law builds on that approach.

For public agencies and developers, earlier decisions could make it easier to coordinate site preparation, construction contracts and financing. The economic gain depends on whether sites actually become available sooner. If disputes over valuation or payment carry over into later stages, the time saved on the acquisition decision could be offset by delays before construction begins.

Farmers could lose bargaining power before compensation is settled Farmland is especially exposed because a household can lose its source of income without having to move. Chris Luong, a partner at CNC Counsel, said the faster procedure could therefore matter more for agricultural plots than for residential property. For farmers, the practical questions are how long they can keep using their land, when compensation arrives and whether a replacement plot can sustain production.

Two consent rules matter here. The earlier implementing decree identifies a route to an acquisition decision before compensation approval when more than 75% of land users agree. Reporting on the adopted law describes a separate mechanism for recovering the remaining land in a negotiated project after an investor has secured agreements covering more than 75% of both the land area and the land users. The distinction matters to developers assembling a site and to households that remain in negotiations after most neighbours have agreed.

Provincial authorities face the hardest decisions on compensation Vietnam's government says the law gives priority to compensation in land with the same use as the land acquired. It also provides for other forms of compensation, including housing or cash, subject to the circumstances and what is available locally. That makes provincial capacity consequential. A same-use plot can help a farming household keep earning, while a cash award leaves the household to find replacement land or another source of income. The options will vary with local land supply.

Policymakers also face a timing issue. The law generally takes effect in July 2027, while the new land price schedules and adjustment coefficients are due to apply from January 1, 2028. For cases that span those dates, households and investors will need clarity on which valuation rules apply. Publishing the basis for each offer and the route for challenging it would help land users assess compensation and give developers a clearer view of likely costs.

The first cases will show whether faster decisions deliver fairer outcomes Hanoi's proposed $28 billion Red River redevelopment shows how much can turn on compensation. Bloomberg reported that about 280,000 people live in the area covered by the project and that city officials proposed higher payments amid resistance. The dispute illustrates the stakes when a project affects homes, livelihoods and neighbourhood ties at the same time. Whether any part of the project can use an accelerated procedure depends on the applicable acquisition and resettlement rules.

The first cases under the revised law should show how provinces record consent, handle objections and sequence possession and payment. For Vietnam, the measure of success is whether priority projects reach construction sooner. For affected households, it is whether they receive compensation and livelihood support in time to replace what they lose. Tracking both outcomes would show whether the reform resolves delays or shifts their cost onto land users.
